entries.333f262bb02cbccdba6cec9370887c97081df4d8: <div sID="gen15871" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Isa.19" sID="Isa.19"/> <div eID="gen15871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15872" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15873" type="x-p"/> As Assyria was a breaking rod to Judah, with which it was smitten, so Egypt was a broken reed, with which it was cheated; and therefore God had a quarrel with them both. We have before read the doom of the Assyrians; now here we have the burden of Egypt, a prophecy concerning that nation, I. That it should be greatly weakened and brought low, and should be as contemptible among the nations as now it was considerable, rendered so by a complication of judgments which God would bring upon them, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.17">ver. 1-17</reference>. II. That at length God's holy religion should be brought into Egypt, and set up there, in part by the Jews that should flee thither for refuge, but more fully by the preachers of the gospel of Christ, through whose ministry churches should be planted in Egypt in the days of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.18-Isa.19.25">ver. 18-25</reference>), which would abundantly balance all the calamities here threatened.
entries.425fab419d40ee89206bfeb9526be0ea1ddaf417: <div eID="gen15873" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15872" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen15874" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of Egypt. Behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it. <hi type="super">2</hi> And I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians: and they shall fight every one against his brother, and every one against his neighbour; city against city, <hi type="italic">and</hi> kingdom against kingdom. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof; and I will destroy the counsel thereof: and they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the Egyptians will I give over into the hand of a cruel lord; and a fierce king shall rule over them, saith the Lord, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up. <hi type="super">6</hi> And they shall turn the rivers far away; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up: the reeds and flags shall wither. <hi type="super">7</hi> The paper reeds by the brooks, by the mouth of the brooks, and every thing sown by the brooks, shall wither, be driven away, and be no <hi type="italic">more.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish. <hi type="super">9</hi> Moreover they that work in fine flax, and they that weave networks, shall be confounded. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices <hi type="italic">and</hi> ponds for fish. <hi type="super">11</hi> Surely the princes of Zoan <hi type="italic">are</hi> fools, the counsel of the wise counsellors of Pharaoh is become brutish: how say ye unto Pharaoh, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? <hi type="super">12</hi> Where <hi type="italic">are</hi> they? where <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy wise <hi type="italic">men?</hi> and let them tell thee now, and let them know what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath purposed upon Egypt. <hi type="super">13</hi> The princes of Zoan are become fools, the princes of Noph are deceived; they have also seduced Egypt, <hi type="italic">even they that are</hi> the stay of the tribes thereof. <hi type="super">14</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof: and they have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof, as a drunken <hi type="italic">man</hi> staggereth in his vomit. <hi type="super">15</hi> Neither shall there be <hi type="italic">any</hi> work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do. <hi type="super">16</hi> In that day shall Egypt be like unto women: and it shall be afraid and fear because of the shaking of the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, which he shaketh over it. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the land of Judah shall be a terror unto Egypt, every one that maketh mention thereof shall be afraid in himself, because of the counsel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, which he hath determined against it. <div eID="gen15874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15875" type="x-p"/> Though the land of Egypt had of old been a house of bondage to the people of God, where they had been ruled with rigour, yet among the unbelieving Jews there still remained much of the humour of their fathers, who said, <hi type="italic">Let us make us a captain and return into Egypt.</hi> Upon all occasions they trusted to Egypt for help (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">ch. xxx. 2</reference>), and thither they fled, in disobedience to God's express command, when things were brought to the last extremity in their own country, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.7">Jer. xliii. 7</reference>. Rabshakeh upbraided Hezekiah with this, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">ch. xxxvi. 6</reference>. While they kept up an alliance with Egypt, and it was a powerful ally, they stood not in awe of the judgments of God; for against them they depended upon Egypt to protect them. Nor did they depend upon the power of God when at anytime they were in distress; but Egypt was their confidence. To prevent all this mischief, Egypt must be mortified, and many ways God here tells them he will take to mortify them. <div eID="gen15875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15876" type="x-p"/> I. The gods of Egypt shall appear to them to be what they always really were, utterly unable to help them, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">v. 1</reference>. "<hi type="italic">The Lord rides upon a cloud, a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt.</hi> As a judge goes in state to the bench to try and condemn the malefactors, or as a general takes the field with his troops to crush the rebels, so shall God come into Egypt with his judgments; and when he comes he will certainly overcome." In all this burden of Egypt here is no mention of any foreign enemy invading them; but God himself will come against them, and raise up the causes of their destruction from among themselves. He comes upon a cloud, above the reach of the opposition or resistance. He comes apace upon a swift cloud; for their judgment lingers not when the time has come. He <hi type="italic">rides upon the wings of the wind,</hi> with a majesty far excelling the greatest pomp and splendour of earthly princes. He <hi type="italic">makes the clouds his chariots,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Ps. xviii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">civ. 3</reference>. When he comes <hi type="italic">the idols of Egypt shall be moved,</hi> shall be removed at his presence, and perhaps be made to fall as Dagon did before the ark. Isis, Osiris, and Apis, those celebrated idols of Egypt, being found unable to relieve their worshippers, shall be disowned and rejected by them. Idolatry had got deeper rooting in Egypt than in any land besides, even the most absurd idolatries; and yet now the idols shall be moved and they shall be ashamed of them. When the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt he <hi type="italic">executed judgments upon the gods of the Egyptians</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.33.4">Num. xxxiii. 4</reference>); no marvel then if, when he comes, they begin to tremble. The Egyptians <hi type="italic">shall seek to the idols,</hi> when they are at their wits' end, and consult <hi type="italic">the charmers and wizards</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">v. 3</reference>); but all in vain; they see their ruin hastening on them notwithstanding. <div eID="gen15876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15877" type="x-p"/> II. The militia of Egypt, that had been famed for their valour, shall be quite dispirited and disheartened. No kingdom in the world was ever in a better method of keeping up a standing army than the Egyptians were; but now their heroes, that used to be celebrated for courage, shall be posted for cowards: <hi type="italic">The heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it,</hi> like wax before the fire (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">v. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">the spirit of Egypt shall fail,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">v. 3</reference>. They shall have no inclination, no resolution, to stand up in defence of their country, their liberty, and property; but shall tamely and ingloriously yield all to the invader and oppressor. The Egyptians <hi type="italic">shall be like women</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">v. 16</reference>); they shall be frightened and put into confusion by the least alarm; even those that dwell in the heart of the country, in the midst of it, and therefore furthest from danger, will be as full of frights as those that are situate on the frontiers. Let not the bold and brave be proud or secure, for God can easily <hi type="italic">cut off the spirit of princes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.12">Ps. lxxvi. 12</reference>) and <hi type="italic">take away their hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job xii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen15877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15878" type="x-p"/> III. The Egyptians shall be embroiled in endless dissensions and quarrels among themselves. There shall be no occasion to bring a foreign force upon them to destroy them; they shall destroy one another (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians.</hi> As these divisions and animosities are their sin, God is not the author of them, they come from men's lusts; but God, as a Judge, permits them for their punishment, and by their destroying differences corrects them for their sinful agreements. Instead of helping one another, and acting each in his place for the common good, <hi type="italic">they shall fight every one against his brother and neighbour,</hi> whom he ought to love as himself—<hi type="italic">city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.</hi> Egypt was then divided into twelve provinces, or dynasties; but Psammetichus, the governor of one of them, by setting them at variance with one another, at length made himself master of them all. A kingdom thus divided against itself would soon be brought to desolation. <hi type="italic">En quo discordiâ cives perduxit miseros!—Oh the wretchedness brought upon a people by their disagreements among themselves!</hi> It is brought to this by <hi type="italic">a perverse spirit,</hi> a spirit of contradiction, which the Lord would mingle, as an intoxicating draught made up of several ingredients, for the Egyptians, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.14">v. 14</reference>. One party shall be for a thing for no other reason than because the other is against it; that is a perverse spirit, which, if it mingle with the public counsels, tends directly to the ruin of the public interests. <div eID="gen15878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15879" type="x-p"/> IV. Their politics shall be all blasted, and turned into foolishness. When God will destroy the nation he will <hi type="italic">destroy the counsel thereof</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">v. 3</reference>), by taking away wisdom from the statesmen (<reference osisRef="Job.12.20">Job xii. 20</reference>), or setting them one against another (as Hushai and Ahithophel), or by his providence breaking their measures even when they seemed well laid; so that the <hi type="italic">princes of Zoan are fools:</hi> they make fools of one another, every one betrays his own folly, and divine Providence makes fools of them all, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">v. 11</reference>. Pharaoh had his wise counsellors. Egypt was famous for such. But their <hi type="italic">counsel has all become brutish;</hi> they have lost all their forecast; one would think they had become idiots, and were bereaved of common sense. Let no man glory then in his own wisdom, nor depend upon that, nor upon the wisdom of those about him; for he that gives understanding can when he please take it away. And from those it is most likely to be taken away that boast of their policy, as Pharaoh's counsellors here did, and, to recommend themselves to places of public trust, boast of their great understanding ("<hi type="italic">I am the son of the wise,</hi> of the God of wisdom, of wisdom itself," says one; "my father was an eminent privy-counsellor of note in his day for wisdom"), or of the antiquity and dignity of their families: "I am," says another, "<hi type="italic">the son of ancient kings.</hi>" The nobles of Egypt boasted much of their antiquity, producing fabulous records of their succession for above 10,000 years. This humour prevailed much among them about this time, as appears by Herodotus, their common boast being that Egypt was some thousands of years more ancient than any other nation. "But <hi type="italic">where are thy wise men?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.12">v. 12</reference>. Let them now show their wisdom by foreseeing what ruin is coming upon their nation, and preventing it, if they can. Let them with all their skill <hi type="italic">know what the Lord of hosts has purposed upon Egypt,</hi> and arm themselves accordingly. Nay, so far are they from doing this that they themselves are, in effect, contriving the ruin of Egypt, and hastening it on, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">The princes of Noph</hi> are not only deceived themselves, but they <hi type="italic">have seduced Egypt,</hi> by putting their kings upon arbitrary proceedings" (by which both themselves and their people were soon undone); "the governors of Egypt, that are the stay and cornerstones of the tribes thereof, are themselves undermining it." It is sad with a people when those that undertake for their safety are helping forward their destruction, and the physicians of the state are her worst disease, when the things that belong to the public peace are so far hidden from the eyes of those that are entrusted with the public counsels that in every thing they blunder and take wrong measures; so here (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have caused Egypt to err in every work thereof.</hi> Every step they took was a false step. They always mistook either the end or the means, and their counsels were all unsteady and uncertain, like the staggerings and stammerings of a drunken man in his vomit, who knows not what he says nor where he goes. See what reason we have to pray for our privy-counsellors and ministers of state, who are the great supports and blessings of the state if God give them a spirit of wisdom, but quite the contrary if he hide their heart from understanding. <div eID="gen15879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15880" type="x-p"/> V. The rod of government shall be turned into the serpent of tyranny and oppression (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Egyptians will I give over into the hand of a cruel lord,</hi> not a foreigner, but one of their own, one that shall rule over them by an hereditary right, but shall be a fierce king and rule them with rigour," either the twelve tyrants that succeeded Sethon, or rather Psammetichus that recovered the monarchy again; for he speaks of one cruel lord. Now the barbarous usage which the Egyptian task masters gave to God's Israel long ago was remembered against them and they were paid in their own coin by another Pharaoh. It is sad with a people when the powers that should be for edification are for destruction, and they are ruined by those by whom they should be ruled, when such as this is the manner of the king, as it is described (<hi type="italic">in terrorem—in order to impress alarm</hi>), <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.11">1 Sam. viii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen15880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15881" type="x-p"/> VI. Egypt was famous for its river Nile, which was its wealth, and strength, and beauty, and was idolized by them. Now it is here threatened that <hi type="italic">the waters shall fail from the sea</hi> and the river shall be <hi type="italic">wasted and dried up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.5">v. 5</reference>. Nature shall not herein favour them as she has done. Egypt was never watered with the rain of heaven (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.18">Zech. xiv. 18</reference>), and therefore the fruitfulness of their country depended wholly upon the overflowing of their river; if that therefore be dried up, their fruitful land will soon be turned into barrenness and their harvests cease: <hi type="italic">Every thing sown by the brooks will wither</hi> of course, will <hi type="italic">be driven away, and be no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.7">v. 7</reference>. If the paper-reeds by the brooks, at the very mouth of them, wither, much more the corn, which lies at a greater distance, but derives its moisture from them. Yet this is not all; the drying up of their rivers is the destruction, 1. Of their fortifications, for they are <hi type="italic">brooks of defence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.6">v. 6</reference>), making the country difficult of access to an enemy. Deep rivers are the strongest lines, and most hardly forced. Pharaoh is said to be a <hi type="italic">great dragon lying in the midst of his rivers,</hi> and guarded by them, bidding defiance to all about him, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.3">Ezek. xxix. 3</reference>. But these <hi type="italic">shall be emptied and dried up,</hi> not by an enemy, as Sennacherib with the <hi type="italic">sole of his foot dried up mighty rivers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.25">ch. xxxvii. 25</reference>), and as Cyrus, who took Babylon by drawing Euphrates into many streams, but by the providence of God, which sometimes <hi type="italic">turns water-springs into dry ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.33">Ps. cvii. 33</reference>. 2. It is the destruction of their fish, which in Egypt was much of their food, witness that base reflection which the children of Israel made (<reference osisRef="Num.11.5">Num. xi. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">We remember the fish which we did eat in Egypt freely.</hi> The drying up of the rivers will <hi type="italic">kill the fish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.29">Ps. cv. 29</reference>), and will thereby ruin those who make it their business, (1.) To catch fish, whether by angling or nets (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.8">v. 8</reference>); they shall <hi type="italic">lament</hi> and <hi type="italic">languish,</hi> for their trade is at an end. There is nothing which the children of this world do more heartily lament than the loss of that which they used to get money by. <hi type="italic">Ploratur lachrymis amissa pecunia veris—Those are genuine tears which are shed over lost money.</hi> (2.) To keep fish, that it may be ready when it is called for. There were those that <hi type="italic">made sluices and ponds for fish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.10">v. 10</reference>), but <hi type="italic">they shall be broken in the purposes thereof;</hi> their business will fail, either for want of water to fill their ponds or for want of fish to replenish their waters. God can find ways to deprive a country even of that which is its staple commodity. The Egyptians may themselves remember <hi type="italic">the fish they have formerly eaten freely,</hi> but now cannot have for money. And that which aggravates the loss of these advantages by the river is that it is their own doing (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall turn the rivers far away.</hi> Their kings and great men, to gratify their own fancy, will drain water from the main river to their own houses and grounds at a distance, preferring their private convenience before the public good, and so by degrees the force of the river is sensibly weakened. Thus many do themselves a greater prejudice at last than they think of, [1.] Who pretend to be wiser than nature, and to do better for themselves than nature has done. [2.] Who consult their own particular interest more than the common good. Such may gratify themselves, but surely they can never satisfy themselves, who to serve a turn contribute to a public calamity, which they themselves, in the long run, cannot avoid sharing in. Herodotus tells us that Pharaoh-Necho (who reigned not long after this), projecting to cut a free passage by water from Nilus into the Red Sea, employed a vast number of men to make a ditch or channel for that purpose, in which attempt he impaired the river, lost 120,000 of his people, and yet left the work unaccomplished. <div eID="gen15881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15882" type="x-p"/> VII. Egypt was famous for the linen manufacture; but that trade shall be ruined. Solomon's merchants traded with Egypt for linen-yarn, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.28">1 Kings x. 28</reference>. Their country produced the best flax and the best hands to work it; but <hi type="italic">those that work in fine flax shall be confounded</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.9">v. 9</reference>), either for want of flax to work on or for want of a demand for that which they have worked or opportunity to export it. The decay of trade weakens and wastes a nation and by degrees brings it to ruin. The trade of Egypt must needs sink, for (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.15">v. 15</reference>) <hi type="italic">there shall not be any work for Egypt</hi> to be employed in; and where there is nothing to be done there is nothing to be got. There shall be a universal stop put to business, <hi type="italic">no work which either head or tail, branch or rush, may do;</hi> nothing for high or low, weak or strong, to do; <hi type="italic">no hire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.8.10">Zech. viii. 10</reference>. Note, The flourishing of a kingdom depends much upon the industry of the people; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> things are likely to do well when all hands are at work, when the head and top-branch do not disdain to labour, and the labour of the tail and rush is not disdained. But when the learned professions are unemployed, the principal merchants have no stocks, and the handicraft tradesmen nothing to do, poverty comes upon a people <hi type="italic">as one that travaileth</hi> and <hi type="italic">as an armed man.</hi> <div eID="gen15882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15883" type="x-p"/> VIII. A general consternation shall seize the Egyptians; they <hi type="italic">shall be afraid and fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">v. 16</reference>), which will be both an evidence of a universal decay and a means and presage of utter ruin. Two things will put them into this fright:—1. What they hear from <hi type="italic">the land of Judah;</hi> that <hi type="italic">shall be a terror to Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">v. 17</reference>. When they hear of the desolations made in Judah by the army of Sennacherib, considering both the near neighbourhood and the strict alliance that was between them and Judah, they will conclude it must be their turn next to become a prey to that victorious army. When their neighbour's house was on fire they could not but see their own in danger; and therefore every one of the Egyptians that makes mention of Judah shall be afraid of himself, expecting the bitter cup shortly to be put into his hands. 2. What they see in their own land. They shall <hi type="italic">fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">because of the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">v. 17</reference>) <hi type="italic">because of the counsel of the Lord of hosts,</hi> which from the shaking of his hand they shall conclude <hi type="italic">he has determined</hi> against Egypt as well as Judah. For, if judgment begin at the house of God, where will it end? <hi type="italic">If this be done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?</hi> See here, (1.) How easily God can make those a terror to themselves that have been, not only secure, but a terror to all about them. It is but shaking his hand over them, or laying it upon some of their neighbours, and the stoutest hearts tremble immediately. (2.) How well it becomes us to fear before God when he does but shake his hand over us, and to humble ourselves under his mighty hand when it does but threaten us, especially when we see his counsel determined against us; for who can change his counsel?
entries.5e74ab83ce1623122f94de21b5898199205d0b15: <div eID="gen15883" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises to Egypt. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 710.)</title> <div sID="gen15884" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction. <hi type="super">19</hi> In that day shall there be an altar to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">20</hi> And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts in the land of Egypt: for they shall cry unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> because of the oppressors, and he shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in that day, and shall do sacrifice and oblation; yea, they shall vow a vow unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and perform <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">22</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal <hi type="italic">it:</hi> and they shall return <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he shall be intreated of them, and shall heal them. <hi type="super">23</hi> In that day shall there be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria, and the Egyptians shall serve with the Assyrians. <hi type="super">24</hi> In that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a blessing in the midst of the land: <hi type="super">25</hi> Whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts shall bless, saying, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance. <div eID="gen15884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15885" type="x-p"/> Out of the thick and threatening clouds of the foregoing prophecy the sun of comfort here breaks forth, and it is the sun of righteousness. Still God has mercy in store for Egypt, and he will show it, not so much by reviving their trade and replenishing their river again as by bringing the true religion among them, calling them to, and accepting them in, the worship of the one only living and true God; and these blessings of grace were much more valuable than all the blessings of nature wherewith Egypt was enriched. We know not of any event in which this prophecy can be thought to have its full accomplishment short of the conversion of Egypt to the faith of Christ, by the preaching (as is supposed) of Mark the Evangelist, and the founding of many Christian churches there, which flourished for many ages. Many prophecies of this book point to the days of the Messiah; and why not this? It is no unusual thing to speak of gospel graces and ordinances in the language of the Old-Testament institutions. And, in these prophecies, those words, <hi type="italic">in that day,</hi> perhaps have not always a reference to what goes immediately before, but have a peculiar significancy pointing at that day which had been so long fixed, and so often spoken of, when the day-spring from on high should visit this dark world. Yet it is not improbable (which some conjecture) that this prophecy was in part fulfilled when those Jews who fled from their own country to take shelter in Egypt, when Sennacherib invaded their land, brought their religion along with them, and, being awakened to great seriousness by the troubles they were in, made an open and zealous profession of it there, and were instrumental to bring many of the Egyptians to embrace it, which was an earnest and specimen of the more plentiful harvest of souls that should be gathered in to God by the preaching of the gospel of Christ. Josephus indeed tells us that Onias the son of Onias the high priest, living an outlaw at Alexandria in Egypt, obtained leave of Ptolemy Philometer, then king, and Cleopatra his queen, to build a temple to the God of Israel, like that at Jerusalem, at Bubastis in Egypt, and pretended a warrant for doing it from this prophecy in Isaiah, that there shall be an <hi type="italic">altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt;</hi> and the service of God, Josephus affirms, continued in it about 333 years, when it was shut up by Paulinus soon after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans; see <hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 13.62-79, and <hi type="italic">Jewish War</hi> 7.426-436. But that temple was all along looked upon by the pious Jews as so great an irregularity, and an affront to the temple at Jerusalem, that we cannot suppose this prophecy to be fulfilled in it. <div eID="gen15885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15886" type="x-p"/> Observe how the conversion of Egypt is here described. <div eID="gen15886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15887" type="x-p"/> I. They shall <hi type="italic">speak the language of Canaan,</hi> the holy language, the scripture-language; they shall not only understand it, but use it (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">v. 18</reference>); they shall introduce that language among them, and converse freely with the people of God, and not, as they used to do, <hi type="italic">by an interpreter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.42.23">Gen. xlii. 23</reference>. Note, Converting grace, by changing the heart, changes the language; <hi type="italic">for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Five cities in Egypt</hi> shall speak this language; so many Jews shall come to reside in Egypt, and they shall so multiply there, that they shall soon replenish five cities, one of which shall be the city of Heres, or of the sun, Heliopolis, where the sun was worshipped, the most infamous of all the cities of Egypt for idolatry; even there shall be a wonderful reformation, they shall speak the language of Canaan. Or it may be taken thus, as we render it—That for every five cities that shall embrace religion there shall be one (a sixth part of the cities of Egypt) that shall reject it, and that shall be called <hi type="italic">a city of destruction,</hi> because it refuses the methods of salvation. <div eID="gen15887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15888" type="x-p"/> II. They shall swear to the Lord of hosts, not only swear by him, giving him the honour of appealing to him, as all nations did to the gods they worshipped; but they shall by a solemn oath and vow devote themselves to his honour and bind themselves to his service. They shall swear to cleave to him with purpose of heart, and shall worship him, not occasionally, but constantly. They shall swear allegiance to him as their King, to Christ, to whom all judgment is committed. <div eID="gen15888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15889" type="x-p"/> III. They shall set up the public worship of God in their land (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">There shall be an altar to the Lord</hi> in the <hi type="italic">midst of the land of Egypt,</hi> an altar on which <hi type="italic">they shall do sacrifice and oblation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.21">v. 21</reference>); therefore it must be understood spiritually. Christ, the great altar, who sanctifies every gift, shall be owned there, and the gospel sacrifices of prayer and praise shall be offered up; for by the law of Moses there was to be no altar for sacrifice but that at Jerusalem. In Christ Jesus all distinction of nations is taken away; and a spiritual altar, a gospel church, in the midst of the land of Egypt, is as acceptable to God as one in the midst of the land of Israel; and spiritual sacrifices of faith and love, and a contrite heart, <hi type="italic">please the Lord better than an ox or bullock.</hi> <div eID="gen15889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15890" type="x-p"/> IV. There shall be a face of religion upon the nation, and an open profession made of it, discernible to all who come among them. Not only in the heart of the country, but even in <hi type="italic">the borders</hi> of it, <hi type="italic">there shall be a pillar,</hi> or pillars, inscribed, <hi type="italic">To Jehovah,</hi> to his honour, as before there had been such pillars set up in honour of false gods. As soon as a stranger entered upon the borders of Egypt he might perceive what god they worshipped. Those that serve God must not be ashamed to own him, but be forward to do any thing that may be for a sign and for a witness to the Lord of hosts. Even in the land of Egypt he had some faithful worshippers, who boasted of their relation to him and made his name their strong tower, or bulwark, on their borders, with which their coasts were fortified against all assailants. <div eID="gen15890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15891" type="x-p"/> V. Being in distress, they shall seek to God, and he shall be found of them; and this <hi type="italic">shall be a sign and a witness for the Lord of hosts</hi> that he is a <hi type="italic">God hearing prayer</hi> to <hi type="italic">all flesh</hi> that <hi type="italic">come to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.20">v. 20</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.65.2">Ps. lxv. 2</reference>. When they cry to God by reason of their oppressors, the cruel lords that shall <hi type="italic">rule over them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">v. 4</reference>) he <hi type="italic">shall be entreated of them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.22">v. 22</reference>); whereas he had told his people Israel, who had made it their own choice to have such a king, that they should <hi type="italic">cry to him by reason of their king,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">would not hear them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.18">1 Sam. viii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen15891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15892" type="x-p"/> VI. They shall have an interest in the great Redeemer. When they were under the oppression of cruel lords perhaps God sometimes raised them up mighty deliverers, as he did for Israel in the days of the judges; and by them, though he had smitten the land, he healed it again; and, upon their return to God in a way of duty, he returned to them in a way of mercy, and repaired the breaches of their tottering state. For repenting Egyptians shall find the same favour with God that repenting Ninevites did. But all these deliverances wrought for them, as those for Israel, were but figures of gospel salvation. Doubtless Jesus Christ is <hi type="italic">the Saviour and the great one</hi> here spoken of, whom God will send the glad tidings of to the Egyptians, and by whom he will <hi type="italic">deliver them out of the hands of their enemies,</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">serve him without fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. Jesus Christ delivered the Gentile nations from the service of dumb idols, and did himself both purchase and preach liberty to the captives. <div eID="gen15892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15893" type="x-p"/> VII. The knowledge of God shall prevail among them, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.21">v. 21</reference>. 1. They shall have the means of knowledge. For many ages in <hi type="italic">Judah only was God known,</hi> for there only were the lively oracles found; but now <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> and his name and will, <hi type="italic">shall be known to Egypt.</hi> Perhaps this may in part refer to the translation of the Old Testament out of Hebrew into Greek by the LXX., which was done at Alexandria in Egypt, by the command of Ptolemy king of Egypt; and it was the first time that the scriptures were translated into any other language. By the help of this (the Grecian monarchy having introduced their language into that country) <hi type="italic">the Lord was known to Egypt,</hi> and a happy omen and means it was of his being further known. 2. They shall have grace to improve those means. It is promised not only that the Lord shall be known to Egypt, but that <hi type="italic">the Egyptians shall know the Lord;</hi> they shall receive and entertain the light granted to them, and shall submit themselves to the power of it. The Lord is known to our nation, and yet I fear there are many of our nation that do not know the Lord. But the promise of the new covenant is that <hi type="italic">all shall know the Lord, from the least even to the greatest,</hi> which promise is sure to all the seed. The effect of this knowledge of God is that <hi type="italic">they shall vow a vow to the Lord and perform it.</hi> For those do not know God aright who either are not willing to come under binding obligations to the Lord or do not make good those obligations. <div eID="gen15893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15894" type="x-p"/> VIII. They shall come into the communion of saints. Being joined to the Lord, they shall be added to the church, and be incorporated with all the saints. 1. All enmities shall be slain. Mortal feuds there had been between Egypt and Assyria; they often made war upon one another; but now <hi type="italic">there shall be a highway between Egypt and Assyria</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.23">v. 23</reference>), a happy correspondence settled between he two nations; they shall trade with one another, and every thing that passes between them shall be friendly. <hi type="italic">The Egyptians shall serve</hi> (shall worship the true God) <hi type="italic">with the Assyrians;</hi> and therefore the Assyrians shall come into Egypt and the Egyptians into Assyria. Note, It becomes those who have communion with the same God, through the same Mediator, to keep up an amicable correspondence with one another. The consideration of our meeting at the same throne of grace, and our serving with each other in the same business of religion, should put an end to all heats and animosities, and knit our hearts to each other in holy love. 2. The Gentile nations shall not only unite with each other in the gospel fold under Christ the great shepherd, but they shall all be united with the Jews. When Egypt and Assyria become partners in serving God <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> shall <hi type="italic">make a third with</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.24">v. 24</reference>); they shall become a <hi type="italic">three-fold cord, not easily broken.</hi> The ceremonial law, which had long been the partition-wall between Jews and Gentiles, shall be taken down, and then they shall become <hi type="italic">one sheep-fold under one shepherd.</hi> Thus united, they shall be <hi type="italic">a blessing in the midst of the land, whom the Lord of hosts shall bless,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.24-Isa.19.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. (1.) Israel shall be a blessing to them all, because of <hi type="italic">them, as concerning the flesh, Christ came,</hi> and they were the natural branches of the good olive, to whom did originally pertain <hi type="italic">its root and fatness,</hi> and the Gentiles were but <hi type="italic">grafted in among them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Rom. xi. 17</reference>. Israel lay between Egypt and Assyria, and was a blessing to them both by bringing them to meet in that word of the Lord which went forth from Jerusalem, and that church which was first set up in the land of Israel. <hi type="italic">Qui conveniunt in aliquo tertio inter se conveniunt—Those who meet in a third meet in each other.</hi> Israel is that third in whom Egypt and Assyria agree, and is therefore a blessing; for those are real and great blessings to their generation who are instrumental to unite those that have been at variance. (2.) They shall all be a blessing to the world: so the Christian church is, made up of Jews and Gentiles; it is the beauty, riches, and support of the world. (3.) They shall all be blessed of the Lord. [1.] They shall all be owned by him as his. Though Egypt was formerly a house of bondage to the people of God, and Assyria an unjust invader of them, all this shall now be forgiven and forgotten, and they shall be as welcome to God as Israel. They are all alike his people whom he takes under his protection. They are formed by him, for they are the <hi type="italic">work of his hands;</hi> not only as <hi type="italic">a</hi> people, but as <hi type="italic">his</hi> people. They are formed for him; for they are his inheritance, precious in his eyes, and dear to him, and from whom he has his rent of honour out of this lower world. [2.] They shall be owned together by him as jointly his, his in concert; they shall all share in one and the same blessing. Note, Those that are united in the love and blessing of God ought, for that reason, to be united to each other in charity.  <chapter eID="Isa.19"/> <div eID="gen15894" type="x-p"/>

entries.33247a64892c57398d0f708c89cc329396a763bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8645"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <div sID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">Is 19:1-25</reference>.<div eID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> The nineteenth and twentieth chapters are connected, but with an interval between. Egypt had been held by an Ethiopian dynasty, Sabacho, Sevechus, or Sabacho II, and Tirhakah, for forty or fifty years. Sevechus (called So, the ally of Hoshea, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>), retired from Lower Egypt on account of the resistance of the priests; and perhaps also, as the Assyrians threatened Lower Egypt. On his withdrawal, Sethos, one of the priestly caste, became supreme, having Tanis ("Zoan") or else Memphis as his capital, 718 B.C.; while the Ethiopians retained Upper Egypt, with Thebes as its capital, under Tirhakah. A third native dynasty was at Sais, in the west of Lower Egypt; to this at a later period belonged Psammetichus, the first who admitted Greeks into Egypt and its armies; he was one of the dodecarchy, a number of petty kings between whom Egypt was divided, and by aid of foreign auxiliaries overcame the rest, 670 B.C. To the divisions at this last time, Gesenius refers <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Is 19:2</reference>; and Psammetichus, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">Is 19:4</reference>, "a cruel lord." The dissensions of the ruling castes are certainly referred to. But the time referred to is much earlier than that of Psammetichus. In <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Is 19:1</reference>, the invasion of Egypt is represented as caused by "the Lord"; and in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">Is 19:17</reference>, "Judah" is spoken of as "a terror to Egypt," which it could hardly have been by itself. Probably, therefore, the Assyrian invasion of Egypt under Sargon, when Judah was the ally of Assyria, and Hezekiah had not yet refused tribute as he did in the beginning of Sennacherib's reign, is meant. That Assyria was in Isaiah's mind appears from the way in which it is joined with Israel and Egypt in the worship of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.24">Is 19:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.25">25</reference>). Thus the dissensions referred to (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Is 19:2</reference>) allude to the time of the withdrawal of the Ethiopians from Lower Egypt, probably not without a struggle, especially with the priestly caste; also to the time when Sethos usurped the throne and entered on the contest with the military caste, by the aid of the town populations: when the Saitic dynasty was another cause of division. Sargon's reign was between 722-715 B.C. answering to 718 B.C., when Sethos usurped his throne [G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8645"/><hi type="bold">1. burden--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.1">Is 13:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon ... cloud--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">18:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come into Egypt--</hi>to inflict vengeance. "Egypt," in Hebrew, Misraim, plural form, to express the two regions of Egypt. Bunsen observes, The title of their kings runs thus: "Lord of Upper and Lower Egypt."<div eID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">idols--</hi>the bull, crocodile, &c. The idols poetically are said to be "moved" with fear at the presence of one mightier than even they were supposed to be (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Ex 12:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.43.12">Jr 43:12</reference>). <div eID="gen14240" type="x-p"/>
entries.b51c089b3e67acdd105b60bd392456c9906f47df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8646"/><div sID="gen14241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8646"/><hi type="bold">2. set--</hi>stir up. Gesenius translates, "arm."<div eID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Egyptians against the Egyptians--</hi>Lower against Upper: and Saitic against both. (See <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Is 3:10</reference>). Newton refers it to the civil wars between Apries and Amasis at the time of Nebuchadnezzar's invasion; also between Tachos, Nectanebus, and the Mendesians, just before Ochus subdued Egypt.<div eID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kingdom against kingdom--</hi>The Septuagint has "nome against nome"; Egypt was divided into forty-two nomes or districts. <div eID="gen14243" type="x-p"/>
entries.d72eab5c0fa4f99cb6519bc950ec64f5aa1fd4ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8647"/><div sID="gen14244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8647"/><hi type="bold">3. spirit--</hi>wisdom, for which Egypt was famed (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.2">Is 31:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.30">1Ki 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.22">Ac 7:22</reference>); answering to "counsel" in the parallel clause.<div eID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fail--</hi>literally, "be poured out," that is, be made void (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">Jr 19:7</reference>). They shall "seek" help from sources that can afford none, "charmers," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Is 8:19</reference>).<div eID="gen14245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">charmers--</hi>literally, "those making a faint sound"; the soothsayers imitated the faint sound which was attributed to the spirits of the dead (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Is 8:19</reference>). <div eID="gen14246" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b8e364fe4091f82968b3a47a24af2a87885c9be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8648"/><div sID="gen14247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8648"/><hi type="bold">4. cruel lord--</hi>"Sargon," in Hebrew it is lords; but plural is often used to express greatness, where, one alone is meant (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.2">Ge 39:2</reference>). The parallel word "king" (singular) proves it. Newton makes the general reference to be to Nebuchadnezzar, and a particular reference to Cambyses, son of Cyrus (who killed the Egyptian god, Apis), and Ochus, Persian conquerors of Egypt, noted for their "fierce cruelty." Gesenius refers it to Psammetichus, who had brought into Egypt Greek and other foreign mercenaries to subdue the other eleven princes of the dodecarchy. <div eID="gen14247" type="x-p"/>
entries.754bba4486743bae6cca0e96a7cd52347fb9973f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8649"/><div sID="gen14248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8649"/><hi type="bold">5. the sea--</hi>the Nile. Physical calamities, it is observed in history, often accompany political convulsions (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.12">Eze 30:12</reference>). The Nile shall "fail" to rise to its wonted height, the result of which will be barrenness and famine. Its "waters" at the time of the overflow resemble "a sea" [Pliny, Natural History, 85.11]; and it is still called El-Bahr," "the sea," by the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Is 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">Jr 51:36</reference>). A public record is kept at Cairo of the daily rise of the water at the proper time of overflow, namely, August: if it rises to a less height than twelve cubits, it will not overflow the land, and famine must be the result. So, also, when it rises higher than sixteen; for the waters are not drained off in time sufficient to sow the seed. <div eID="gen14248" type="x-p"/>
entries.0caa9c1da93ff3692acf564e755b87820de0f1f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8650"/><div sID="gen14249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8650"/><hi type="bold">6. they shall turn the rivers--</hi>rather, "the streams shall become putrid"; that is, the artificial streams made for irrigation shall become stagnant and offensive when the waters fail [Maurer]. Horsley, with the Septuagint, translates, "And waters from the sea shall be drunk"; by the failure of the river water they shall be reduced to sea water.<div eID="gen14249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brooks of defence--</hi>rather, "canals of Egypt"; "canals," literally, "Niles," Nile canals, the plural of the Egyptian term for the great river. The same Hebrew word, Matzor, whence comes Mitzraim, expresses Egypt, and a place of "defense." Horsley, as English Version translates it, "embanked canals,"<div eID="gen14250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reeds ... flags--</hi>the papyrus. "Reed and rush"; utter withering. <div eID="gen14251" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa443ecd5797316ba42e40fb332953dcc700d4c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8651"/><div sID="gen14252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8651"/><hi type="bold">7. paper-reeds--</hi>rather, pastures, literally, "places naked" of wood, and famed for rich herbage, on the banks of the Nile [Gesenius]. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">Ge 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.10">De 11:10</reference>. Horsley translates, "nakedness upon the river," descriptive of the appearance of a river when its bottom is bare and its banks stripped of verdure by long drought: so Vulgate.<div eID="gen14252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the brooks--</hi>the river.<div eID="gen14253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mouth--</hi>rather, "the source" [Vulgate]. "Even close to the river's side vegetation shall be so withered as to be scattered in the shape of powder by the wind" (English Version, "driven away") [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14254" type="x-p"/>
entries.d047c48072e0fce98eaa18e651734b0b649e751b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8652"/><div sID="gen14255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8652"/><hi type="bold">8. fishers--</hi>The Nile was famed for fish (<reference osisRef="Num.11.5">Nu 11:5</reference>); many would be thrown out of employment by the failure of fishes.<div eID="gen14255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angle--</hi>a hook. Used in the "brooks" or canals, as the "net" was in "the waters" of the river itself. <div eID="gen14256" type="x-p"/>
entries.5237365750c1a27f0a002e88778a76131bf003f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8653"/><div sID="gen14257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8653"/><hi type="bold">9. fine flax--</hi>Gesenius, for "fine," translates, "combed"; fine "linen" was worn by the rich only (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.19">Lu 16:19</reference>). Egypt was famous for it (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.31">Ex 9:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.28">1Ki 10:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.16">Pr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.7">Eze 27:7</reference>). The processes of its manufacture are represented on the Egyptian tombs. Israel learned the art in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.36">Ex 26:36</reference>). The cloth now found on the mummies was linen, as is shown by the microscope. Wilkinson mentions linen from Egypt which has five hundred forty (or two hundred seventy double) threads in one inch in the warp; whereas some modern cambric has but a hundred sixty [Barnes].<div eID="gen14257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">networks--</hi>rather, white cloth (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.6">Es 1:6</reference>; 8:16). <div eID="gen14258" type="x-p"/>
entries.f632e6a9277d1bfea60a20a22ea1c18ae47148fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8654"/><div sID="gen14259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8654"/><hi type="bold">10. in the purposes--</hi>rather, "the foundations," that is, "the nobles shall be broken" or brought low: so <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Is 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Is 19:13</reference>, "The princes--the stay of the tribes. The Arabs call a prince "a pillar of the people" [Maurer]. "Their weaving-frames" [Horsley]. "Dykes" [Barnes].<div eID="gen14259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all that make sluices, &c.--</hi>"makers of dams," made to confine the waters which overflow from the Nile in artificial fish-ponds [Horsley]. "Makers of gain," that is, the common people who have to earn their livelihood, as opposed to the "nobles" previously [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14260" type="x-p"/>
entries.06de219bf13cf32d027916fc293bbae2a72a6b8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8655"/><div sID="gen14261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8655"/><hi type="bold">11. Zoan--</hi>The Greeks called it Tanis, a city of Lower Egypt, east of the Tanitic arms of the Nile, now San; it was one the Egyptian towns nearest to Palestine (<reference osisRef="Num.13.22">Nu 13:22</reference>), the scene of Moses' miracles (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.12">Psa 78:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.43">43</reference>). It, or else Memphis, was the capital under Sethos.<div eID="gen14261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am ... son of the wise ... kings--</hi>Ye have no advice to suggest to Pharaoh in the crisis, notwithstanding that ye boast of descent from wise and royal ancestors. The priests were the usual "counsellors" of the Egyptian king. He was generally chosen from the priestly caste, or, if from the warrior caste, he was admitted into the sacred order, and was called a priest. The priests are, therefore, meant by the expression, "son of the wise, and of ancient kings"; this was their favorite boast (Herodotus, 2.141; compare <reference osisRef="Amos.7.14">Am 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.23.6">Ac 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Php 3:5</reference>). "Pharaoh" was the common name of all the kings: Sethos, probably, is here meant. <div eID="gen14262" type="x-p"/>
entries.f794d910e70f95f2c87b516812edfd4870dd9ef0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8656"/><div sID="gen14263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8656"/><hi type="bold">12. let them know--</hi>that is, How is it that, with all their boast of knowing the future [Diodorus, 1.81], they do not know what Jehovah of hosts ... <div eID="gen14263" type="x-p"/>
entries.debaa04c6952e24e137626d839c67d1929f3f0a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8657"/><div sID="gen14264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8657"/><hi type="bold">13. Noph--</hi>called also Moph; Greek, Memphis (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.6">Ho 9:6</reference>); on the western bank of the Nile, capital of Lower Egypt, second only to Thebes in all Egypt: residence of the kings, until the Ptolemies removed to Alexandria; the word means the "port of the good" [Plutarch]. The military caste probably ruled in it: "they also are deceived," in fancying their country secure from Assyrian invasion.<div eID="gen14264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stay of ... tribes--</hi>rather, "corner-stone of her castes" [Maurer], that is, the princes, the two ruling castes, the priests and the warriors: image from a building which rests mainly on its corner-stones (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.10">Is 19:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Nu 24:17</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Judg.20.2">Jud 20:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.28">1Sa 14:28</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.4">Zec 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen14265" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3e8fe8f009ee65e485a6610f48a447210c2b3c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8658"/><div sID="gen14266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8658"/><hi type="bold">14. err in every work thereof--</hi>referring to the anarchy arising from their internal feuds. Horsley translates, "with respect to all His (God's) work"; they misinterpreted God's dealings at every step. "Mingled" contains the same image as "drunken"; as one mixes spices with wine to make it intoxicating (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Is 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.2">Pr 9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">5</reference>), so Jehovah has poured among them a spirit of giddiness, so that they are as helpless as a "drunken man." <div eID="gen14266" type="x-p"/>
entries.c56855c602c91360e49383633ddf8efa21819dde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8659"/><div sID="gen14267" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8659"/><hi type="bold">15. work for Egypt--</hi>nothing which Egypt can do to extricate itself from the difficulty.<div eID="gen14267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head or tail--</hi>high or low (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.11-Isa.19.15">Is 19:11-15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.19.8-Isa.19.10">Is 19:8-10</reference>).<div eID="gen14268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branch or rush--</hi>the lofty palm branch or the humble reed (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.14">Is 9:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">10:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">34</reference>). <div eID="gen14269" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6342f4a76509525e78ba409d7aba4ce4d6167cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8660"/><div sID="gen14270" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8660"/><hi type="bold">16. like ... women--</hi>timid and helpless (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">Jr 51:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.13">Na 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen14270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shaking of ... hand--</hi>His judgments by means of the invaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen14271" type="x-p"/>
entries.7043275ea295ae1a86f8166969fb4c647da07fe4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8661"/><div sID="gen14272" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8661"/><hi type="bold">17. Judah ... terror unto Egypt--</hi>not by itself: but at this time Hezekiah was the active subordinate ally of Assyria in its invasion of Egypt under Sargon. Similarly to the alliance of Judah with Assyria here is <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>, where Josiah takes the field against Pharaoh-nechoh of Egypt, probably as ally of Assyria against Egypt [G. V. Smith]. Vitringa explains it that Egypt in its calamities would remember that prophets of Judah had foretold them, and so Judah would be "a terror unto Egypt."<div eID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thereof--</hi>of Judah.<div eID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it--</hi>Egypt. <div eID="gen14274" type="x-p"/>
entries.eff6cb72067c0cf1caebd836a63f719d6d8910be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8662"/><div sID="gen14275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8662"/><hi type="bold">18-22. In that day, &c.--</hi>Suffering shall lead to repentance. Struck with "terror" and "afraid" (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">Is 19:17</reference>) because of Jehovah's judgments, Egypt shall be converted to Him: nay, even Assyria shall join in serving Him; so that Israel, Assyria, and Egypt, once mutual foes, shall be bound together by the tie of a common faith as one people. So a similar issue from other prophecies (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Is 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">23:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">five cities--</hi>that is, several cities, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Is 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.17">30:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.34">Ge 43:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.8">Le 26:8</reference>. Rather, five definite cities of Lower Egypt (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">Is 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.4">30:4</reference>), which had close intercourse with the neighboring Jewish cities [Maurer]; some say, Heliopolis, Leontopolis (else Diospolis), Migdol, Daphne (Tahpanes), and Memphis.<div eID="gen14276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">language of Canaan--</hi>that is, of the Hebrews in Canaan, the language of revelation; figuratively for, They shall embrace the Jewish religion: so "a pure language" and conversion to God are connected in <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>; as also the first confounding and multiplication of languages was the punishment of the making of gods at Babel, other than the One God. Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.4">Ac 2:4</reference>) was the counterpart of Babel: the separation of nations is not to hinder the unity of faith; the full realization of this is yet future (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.21">Joh 17:21</reference>). The next clause, "swear to the Lord of Hosts," agrees with this view; that is, bind themselves to Him by solemn covenant (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">Is 45:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.16">65:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">De 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen14277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">city of destruction--</hi>Onias; "city of the sun," that is, On, or Heliopolis; he persuaded Ptolemy Philometer (149 B.C.) to let him build a temple in the prefecture (nome) of Heliopolis, on the ground that it would induce Jews to reside there, and that the very site was foretold by Isaiah six hundred years before. The reading of the Hebrew text is, however, better supported, "city of destruction"; referring to Leontopolis, the site of Onias' temple: which casts a reproach on that city because it was about to contain a temple rivalling the only sanctioned temple, that at Jerusalem. Maurer, with some manuscripts, reads "city of defense" or "deliverance"; namely, Memphis, or some such city, to which God was about to send "a saviour" (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.20">Is 19:20</reference>), to "deliver them." <div eID="gen14278" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a641faf26fae3e391f3d370a4a1c51fe350ddb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8667"/><div sID="gen14290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8667"/><hi type="bold">23. highway--</hi>free communication, resting on the highest basis, the common faith of both (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Is 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.16">Is 11:16</reference>). Assyria and Egypt were joined under Alexander as parts of his empire: Jews and proselytes from both met at the feasts of Jerusalem. A type of gospel times to come.<div eID="gen14290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">serve with--</hi>serve Jehovah with the Assyrians. So "serve" is used absolutely (<reference osisRef="Job.36.11">Job 36:11</reference>). <div eID="gen14291" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a1b4a6a818c3cdca26e03f2c76da55e293dcc39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8668"/><div sID="gen14292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8668"/><hi type="bold">24. third--</hi>The three shall be joined as one nation.<div eID="gen14292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blessing--</hi>the source of blessings to other nations, and the object of their benedictions.<div eID="gen14293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of the land--</hi>rather, "earth" (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>). Judah is designed to be the grand center of the whole earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>). <div eID="gen14294" type="x-p"/>
entries.6606bf40fb4ad58b0491c5efc1a95d3981b6e651: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8669"/><div sID="gen14295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8669"/><hi type="bold">25. Whom--</hi>rather, "Which," namely, "the land," or "earth," that is, the people of it [Maurer].<div eID="gen14295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my people--</hi>the peculiar designation of Israel, the elect people, here applied to Egypt to express its entire admission to religious privileges (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.24-Rom.9.26">Ro 9:24-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen14296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work of my hands--</hi>spiritually (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Ho 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.19"/>

entries.20b9176356a22f7689f86f4505626a474397452a: <div eID="gen27277" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27278" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27279" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27279" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27278" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27280" type="x-p"/> Prophecy concerning Egypt, in which her lamentable condition under the Babylonians, Persians, etc., Is forcibly pointed out, vv. 1-17. The true religion shall be propagated in Egypt; referring primarily to the great spread of Judaism in that country in the reign of the Ptolemies, and ultimately to its reception of the Gospel in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18-Isa.19.22">Isa 19:18-22</reference>. Profound peace between Egypt, Assyria, and Israel, and their blessed condition under the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23-Isa.19.25">Isa 19:23-25</reference>. <div eID="gen27280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27281" type="x-p"/> Not many years after the destruction of Sennacherib's army before Jerusalem, by which the Egyptians were freed from the yoke with which they were threatened by so powerful an enemy, who had carried on a successful war of three years' continuance against them; the affairs of Egypt were again thrown into confusion by intestine broils among themselves, which ended in a perfect anarchy, that lasted some few years. This was followed by an aristocracy, or rather tyranny, of twelve princes, who divided the country between them, and at last by the sole dominion of Psammitichus, which he held for fifty-four years. Not long after that followed the invasion and conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, and then by the Persians under Cambyses, the son of Cyrus. The yoke of the Persians was so grievous, that the conquest of the Persians by Alexander may well be considered as a deliverance to Egypt; especially as he and his successors greatly favored the people and improved the country. To all these events the prophet seems to have had a view in this chapter; and in particular, from <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Isa 19:18</reference>, the prophecy of the propagation of the true religion in Egypt seems to point to the flourishing state of Judaism in that country, in consequence of the great favor shown to the Jews by the Ptolemies. Alexander himself settled a great many Jews in his new city Alexandria, granting them privileges equal to those of the Macedonians. The first Ptolemy, called Soter, carried great numbers of them thither, and gave them such encouragement that still more of them were collected there from different parts; so that Philo reckons that in his time there were a million of Jews in that country. These worshipped the God of their fathers; and their example and influence must have had a great effect in spreading the knowledge and worship of the true God through the whole country. See Bp. Newton on the Prophecies, Dissert. xii. <div eID="gen27281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27282" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27283" type="x-p"/> The burden of Egypt - That is, the prophet's declaration concerning Egypt.
entries.7f51c04b2631986524170ac89ab5095a27cf00b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27284" type="x-p"/> They shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards - And thei schul asken their symulacres, and their debynouris, and their devyl clepers, and their devyl sacristers. - Old Bible. The import of the original words has already been given where they occur in the Pentateuch. See <reference osisRef="Deu.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference>, etc.
entries.bb885d21a780c9ef8dd7e7178b1fb05f6fa7f34e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27285" type="x-p"/> A cruel lord "Cruel lords" - Nebuchadnezzar in the first place, and afterwards the whole succession of Persian kings, who in general were hard masters, and grievously oppressed the country. Note, that for קשה kasheh, lord, a MS. reads קשים kashim, lords, agreeable to which is the rendering of the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate.
entries.85c2e2a5aa3f8c1f0a22dd0df3de2eb20df6fbda: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27286" type="x-p"/> The river shall be wasted and dried up - The Nile shall not overflow its banks; and if no inundation, the land must become barren. For, as there is little or no rain in Egypt, its fertility depends on the overflowing of the Nile.
entries.6a771c1870c74cb8c106dc4402343c9dbf13e496: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27287" type="x-p"/> Shall turn the rivers far away "Shall become putrid" - האזניחו heeznichu. This sense of the word, which Simonis gives in his Lexicon, from the meaning of it in Arabic, suits the place much better than any other interpretation hitherto given; and that the word in Hebrew had some such signification, is probable from <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.19">2Chr 29:19</reference>, where the Vulgate renders it by polluit, polluted, and the Targum, by profaned, and made abominable, which the context in that place seems plainly to require. The form of the verb here is very irregular; and the rabbins and grammarians seem to give no probable account of it.
entries.eca371784666fdc670ada139bcbaece0b66d2839: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27288" type="x-p"/> The fishers also "And the fishers" - There was great plenty of fish in Egypt; see <reference osisRef="Num.11.5">Num 11:5</reference>. "The Nile," says Diodorus, lib. i., "abounds with incredible numbers of all sorts of fish." And much more the lakes. So Egmont, Pococke, etc.
entries.b6965eb47deb1db35eabeeccdec3bf16f2d41f1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27289" type="x-p"/> They that work in fine flax - פשתים שריקות pishtim sericoth, heckled flax, i.e., flax dressed on the heckle, or comb used for that purpose. The Vulgate uses the word pectentes, combing. <div eID="gen27289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27290" type="x-p"/> They that weave networks shall be confounded - And confounden schul ben that wrogten flax, plattinge and webynge sotel thingis. - Old MS. Bible.
entries.60b54b17cc64d54740203e4bc3e7ee7c8d45fe95: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27291" type="x-p"/> And they shall be broken, etc. "Her stores" - שתתיה shathotheyha, αποθηκαι, granaries. - Aquila. <div eID="gen27291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27292" type="x-p"/> All that make sluices and ponds for fish "All that make a gain of pools for fish" - This obscure line is rendered by different interpreters in very different manners. Kimchi explains אגמי agmey as if it were the same with אגמה agemah, from <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">Job 30:25</reference>, in which he is followed by some of the rabbins, and supported by the Septuagint: and שכר secher, which I translate gain, and which some take for nets or enclosures, the Septuagint render by ζυθον, strong drink or beer, which it is well known was much used in Egypt; and so likewise the Syriac, retaining the Hebrew word שכרא sekra. I submit these very different interpretations to the reader's judgment. The Version of the Septuagint is as follows: Και παντες οἱ ποιουντες τον ζυθον λυπηθησονται, και τας ψυχας πονεσουσι· "And all they that make barley wine shall mourn, and be grieved in soul."
entries.7ceac8cc05eff1fd84cd3255a9ac53d3b234d0b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27293" type="x-p"/> The counsel of the wise counselors of Pharaoh is become brutish "Have counseled a brutish counsel" - The sentence as it now stands in the Hebrew, is imperfect: it wants the verb. Archbishop Secker conjectures that the words יועצי פרעה yoatsey pharoh should be transposed; which would in some degree remove the difficulty. But it is to be observed, that the translator of the Vulgate seems to have found in his copy the verb יעצו yaatsu added after פרעה pharoh: Sapientes consiliarii Pharaonis dederunt consilium insipiens, "The wise counsellors of Pharaoh gave unwise counsel." This is probably the true reading: it is perfectly agreeable to the Hebrew idiom, makes the construction of the sentence clear, and renders the transposition of the words above mentioned unnecessary. - L.
entries.c9c457a7d69f4299a3356ef60f6ca8b12a0bf849: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> "Let them come" - Here too a word seems to have been left out of the text. After חכמיך chochameycha, thy wise men, two MSS., one ancient, add יבאו yibu, let them come; which, if we consider the form and construction of the sentence, has very much the appearance of being genuine: otherwise the connective conjunction at the beginning of the next member is not only superfluous but embarrassing. See also the Version of the Septuagint, in which the same deficiency is manifest. <div eID="gen27293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27294" type="x-p"/> Let them tell thee now "And let them declare" - For ידעו yidu, let them know, perhaps we ought to read יודיעו yodiu, let them make known. - Secker. The Septuagint and Vulgate favor this reading, ειπατωισαν, let them declare.
entries.0ffc89f05b8f67de984593ddd21c0353a68f2a55: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27295" type="x-p"/> Are deceived "They have caused," etc. - The text has וחתעו vehithu, And they have caused to err. Fifty of Kennicott's MSS., fifty-three of De Rossi's, and one of my own, ancient, thirty-two editions, and the Vulgate and Chaldee. omit the ו vau, and. <div eID="gen27295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27296" type="x-p"/> Stay "Pillars" - פנת pinnath, to be pointed as plural pinnoth, without doubt. So Grotius, and so the Chaldee.
entries.40c365705e138410e4d6c19f22b04e35ab53c35d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27297" type="x-p"/> In the midst thereof - בקרבם bekirbam; so the Septuagint, and perhaps more correctly." - Secker. So likewise the Chaldee.
entries.5bf16e6fa86ea17df583fc19d926e41067d2d2b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27298" type="x-p"/> The head or tail, branch or rush - R. D. Kimchi says, there are some who suppose that these words mean the dragon's head and tail; and refer to all those who are conversant in astronomy, astrology, etc.
entries.34f88683c7cee9306aca26b063ebc00ba78992c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen27298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27299" type="x-p"/> Shall Egypt be "The Egyptians shall be" - יהיו yihyu, they shall be, plural, MS. Bodl. Septuagint, and Chaldee. This is not proposed as an emendation, for either form is proper.
entries.9a6a6e14f04efe5f0571d25468c679392cbd9191: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27300" type="x-p"/> And the land of Judah - The threatening hand of God will be held out and shaken over Egypt, from the side of Judea; through which the Assyrians will march to invade it. It signifies that kind of terror that drives one to his wit's end, that causes him to reel like a drunken man, to be giddy through astonishment. Such is the import of חג chag, and חגה chagah. Five MSS. and two editions have לחגה lechagah.
entries.030c3f2fb5c83f11e78889836762fe03797e68f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen27300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27301" type="x-p"/> The city of destruction "The city of the sun" - עיר החרס ir hacheres. This passage is attended with much difficulty and obscurity. First, in regard to the true reading. It is well known that Onias applied it to his own views, either to procure from the king of Egypt permission to build his temple in the Hieropolitan Nome, or to gain credit and authority to it when built; from the notion which he industriously propagated, that Isaiah had in this place prophesied of the building of such a temple. He pretended that the very place where it should be built was expressly named by the prophet, עיר החרס ir hacheres, the city of the sun. This possibly may have been the original reading.
